title: Supply
outcomes: Explain the meaning of supply and distinguish it from stock.
List the determinants of supply and state the law of supply with its exception.
Distinguish movements along the supply curve from shifts of the curve.
Classify, measure (percentage, point, arc) and explain the determinants of elasticity of supply; find market equilibrium.

meta.exam_tip: MCQs often test the shift-vs-movement distinction (tax, subsidy, technology), the five types of supply elasticity and an Es calculation. The straight-line intercept rule is a quick win.

concepts.title: Meaning of supply
body: Supply is the quantity of a good or service that producers are willing and able to offer for sale at various prices during a given period. Sellers may be individuals, firms or governments.

Three points: (1) supply is what is offered for sale, not necessarily what is actually sold — some of it may remain unsold; (2) it needs both willingness and ability to supply, and the cost of production mainly decides the ability; (3) supply is a flow — so much per day, week or year.

Supply differs from stock. Stock is the total quantity available with sellers at a point of time; supply is the part of it offered for sale at a given price. For perishable goods (fresh fish, flowers), supply tends to equal stock because they cannot be held back; for durable goods, sellers can keep part of the stock off the market if the price is low.
concepts.analogy: A mango seller's whole basket is his stock; the mangoes he puts on the cart at today's price are his supply.
concepts.work: Inventory (stock) appears in the balance sheet; how much of it the company releases to the market at a given price is a supply decision — a link CAs see in working-capital reviews.

concepts.title: Determinants of supply
body: (1) Price of the good — other things equal, a higher relative price makes production more profitable and raises quantity supplied. (2) Prices of related goods — if other goods a firm could produce become dearer, it shifts resources to them and supply of this good falls (a farmer switches from wheat to mustard when mustard prices rise). (3) Prices of factors of production — higher wages, raw-material or energy costs raise cost of production and reduce supply; cheaper inputs increase it.

(4) State of technology — better technology lowers cost per unit and increases supply. (5) Government policy — taxes (such as excise or GST) raise costs and reduce supply; subsidies lower costs and increase supply; quotas, licensing and regulation can restrict supply. (6) Nature of competition and size of the industry — under competition, supply tends to be larger than under monopoly. (7) Expectations — if prices are expected to rise, sellers may hold back supply now; expected falls lead them to sell more now. (8) Number of sellers — more firms in the market mean larger market supply. Other influences include natural factors such as weather for farm products.
concepts.analogy: Price is the accelerator for supply; costs, taxes and technology decide how powerful the engine is.
concepts.work: Cost audits and margin analysis by CAs explain shifts in a client's supply capacity: a rise in input costs or a new tax shows up as reduced willingness to supply at the old price.

concepts.title: The law of supply: schedule and curve
body: Producers are ready to sell a unit if the price at least covers the cost of producing that extra unit; the bigger the gap between price and that cost, the greater their willingness to supply.

Law of supply: other things remaining constant, the quantity of a good offered for sale rises as its price rises and falls as its price falls — a direct (positive) relationship. Reason: a higher price means higher profits and a stronger incentive to produce and sell.

A supply schedule tabulates prices and the quantities offered. The supply curve plots it and slopes upward from left to right. It shows at the same time the most that suppliers will offer at each price and the minimum price needed to coax out each quantity.
Market supply is the horizontal sum of all individual firms' supplies at each price; it depends on everything that affects individual supply plus the number of firms.

Exception: the supply of labour at very high wages may fall — workers prefer more leisure once they earn enough (backward-bending supply of labour). Time also matters: supply is harder to raise in the short run than in the long run.
concepts.analogy: A higher price is like a bigger reward at a quiz — more people raise their hands.
concepts.work: Capacity planning in manufacturing companies follows the supply curve: when realised prices rise, finance teams model the profitability of running extra shifts.

concepts.title: Movement along vs shift of the supply curve
body: A change in the good's own price, other things constant, causes a movement along the same supply curve — a change in quantity supplied. A rise in price → expansion (extension) of supply, an upward movement along the curve; a fall in price → contraction of supply, a downward movement.

A change in any other determinant — input prices, technology, taxes and subsidies, prices of related goods, expectations, number of firms — shifts the whole supply curve. A rightward shift is an increase in supply: more is offered at each price (or the same quantity at a lower price). A leftward shift is a decrease in supply: less is offered at each price.
Examples: a new labour-saving machine shifts supply right; a rise in the GST rate or in diesel prices shifts supply left; a crop failure shifts farm supply left.
concepts.analogy: Moving along the supply curve is a factory running faster or slower on the same machines; a shift is the factory getting new machines (right) or losing some (left).
concepts.work: When explaining a fall in a client's output to auditors or lenders, CAs separate "we chose to sell less because prices fell" (movement) from "our costs rose so we can offer less at any price" (shift).

concepts.title: Elasticity of supply: meaning and types
body: Price elasticity of supply (Es) measures how much quantity supplied responds to a change in price: Es = % change in quantity supplied ÷ % change in price = (Δq/q) × (p/Δp). Because supply curves slope upward, Es is normally positive.

Types: perfectly inelastic (Es = 0) — quantity does not change, vertical supply curve (e.g. paintings of a dead artist, land in a city centre in the short run); relatively less elastic (0 < Es < 1) — quantity changes less than proportionately; unitary elastic (Es = 1) — equal proportionate change, the dividing line; relatively greater elastic (Es > 1) — quantity changes more than proportionately; perfectly elastic (Es = ∞) — horizontal curve: nothing is offered below the price, and any quantity is offered at it.
A useful rule for straight-line supply curves: a line through the origin has Es = 1 at every point; a line that cuts the price (Y) axis has Es > 1; a line that cuts the quantity (X) axis has Es < 1.
concepts.analogy: Elastic supply is a tap that opens wide with a small twist; inelastic supply is a rusty tap that barely moves however hard you turn it.
concepts.work: Commodity analysts and CAs in agri-finance know that farm supply is inelastic within a season — prices swing sharply because quantity cannot respond until the next sowing.

concepts.title: Measuring elasticity of supply
body: Percentage method: Es = (Δq/q) ÷ (Δp/p), using the original price and quantity as base.
Point method: Es = (dq/dp) × (p/q), where dq/dp is the derivative of the supply function. For a linear supply q = c + dP, dq/dp = d, so Es = d × P/q.

Arc method (mid-point) between two prices: Es = [(Q2 − Q1) ÷ (Q2 + Q1)] × [(P2 + P1) ÷ (P2 − P1)], where P1, Q1 are original and P2, Q2 new values. It gives the same answer whichever direction the price moves.
concepts.analogy: Same three rulers as for demand — only the sign is normally positive because price and quantity move together.
concepts.work: Analysts estimate supply elasticity when forecasting how fast competitors will add capacity after a price rise.

concepts.title: Determinants of elasticity of supply
body: (1) Behaviour of costs as output expands — if costs rise sharply, supply is less elastic; if costs stay roughly constant, it is elastic. (2) Complexity and time needed to produce — aircraft and ships have less elastic supply than motorbikes. (3) Time period — the longer the period, the more elastic; in the long run new plants are built and new firms enter. (4) Number of producers and ease of entry — many competing producers and low entry barriers make supply more elastic. (5) Spare capacity — firms working below full capacity can expand output without extra cost, so supply is more elastic.

(6) Availability of inputs — if key raw materials are easy and cheap to obtain, supply is elastic. (7) Stocks and storability — firms with stocks of materials and finished goods, and goods that can be stored cheaply without losing value, have more elastic supply. (8) Ease of factor substitution — commonly available, easily substitutable inputs make supply elastic; scarce, specialised or long-training inputs (doctors, chartered accountants) make it inelastic. (9) Mobility of factors — if capital and labour can switch easily between products (a printing press moving from magazines to greeting cards), supply is more elastic. (10) Expectations — if sellers expect prices to rise further, they respond less to a current price rise.
concepts.analogy: A street food stall can double its output tomorrow (elastic); a shipyard needs years (inelastic).
concepts.work: Supply of qualified CAs is itself inelastic in the short run — years of training — which is why their fees rise quickly when demand spikes, for example during audit season or new compliance requirements.

concepts.title: Equilibrium price and social efficiency (link to demand)
body: The equilibrium (market-clearing) price is where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied — the intersection of the demand and supply curves. Above it there is excess supply, which pushes price down; below it there is excess demand, which pushes price up. This is why microeconomics is also called price theory.

Social efficiency in a market is the total of consumer surplus and producer surplus. Producer surplus is what sellers receive above the minimum price at which they would have been willing to supply each unit — the region lying over the supply curve and under the market price. A competitive equilibrium maximises the sum of the two.
concepts.analogy: Equilibrium is the point where a tug-of-war between buyers and sellers stops moving.
concepts.work: Fair-value measurement and transfer pricing both ask "what price would a willing buyer and willing seller agree on?" — the market-clearing idea in professional practice.

illustrations.title: Market supply from individual supply schedules
illustrations.q: Three firms supply a product. Derive the market supply schedule and comment.

solution.text: Market supply rises from 5 units at ₹10 to 92 units at ₹50 — the law of supply. Firm 3 starts supplying only at ₹30, showing that higher prices also bring in higher-cost producers.

illustrations.title: Elasticity of supply — percentage method
illustrations.q: When the price of a toy rises from ₹500 to ₹550, the quantity supplied rises from 2,400 to 3,000 units a month. Find Es and classify.

solution.text: % change in q = 600 ÷ 2,400 = 25%; % change in p = 50 ÷ 500 = 10%. Es = 25 ÷ 10 = 2.5. Supply is relatively greater elastic (Es > 1).

illustrations.title: Point elasticity from a supply function
illustrations.q: The supply function is q = −200 + 30P. Find Es at P = ₹20 and P = ₹40. Then find Es at P = ₹20 for the supply function q = 25P and comment.

solution.text: For q = −200 + 30P, dq/dp = 30: Es = 1.5 at ₹20 and 1.2 at ₹40 — elastic, falling towards 1 as price rises. This line cuts the price axis (at P ≈ 6.67), so Es > 1 throughout. For q = 25P, a line through the origin, Es = 1 at every price.

Es for a line through the origin

illustrations.title: Arc elasticity of supply
illustrations.q: At ₹45 a kg, 600 kg of paneer is supplied; at ₹60, 900 kg. Find arc elasticity of supply.

illustrations.title: Equilibrium price from demand and supply functions
illustrations.q: Qd = 500 − 10P and Qs = 50 + 5P. Find the equilibrium price and quantity, and the excess demand or supply at ₹20 and ₹40.

solution.text: Excess demand at ₹20 pushes the price up; excess supply at ₹40 pushes it down — until the market clears at ₹30.

jobs.title: Why did vegetable prices spike?
jobs.role: CA in a food-processing company — procurement finance
jobs.situation: Tomato prices doubled in two weeks after heavy rains. Management asks why suppliers did not simply supply more.
steps: Identify the shift: rain damage reduced supply — a leftward shift of the supply curve.
Explain short-run inelasticity: crops cannot be grown in two weeks, so quantity cannot respond to the higher price.
Plan: long-term contracts with farmers, storage and processing capacity (tomato puree) to reduce exposure.
jobs.takeaway: Farm supply is inelastic in the short run; price shocks are large until the next harvest.

jobs.title: Impact of a subsidy on an EV maker's supply
jobs.role: CA in industry — strategy and planning
jobs.situation: The government announces a production-linked incentive per electric scooter.
steps: A subsidy lowers effective cost per unit — the supply curve shifts right.
Estimate the firm's supply elasticity: spare capacity and available battery supply decide how fast output can rise.
Model the new output and the incentive receivable, and the conditions attached.
jobs.takeaway: Subsidies shift supply right; how much output actually rises depends on elasticity of supply.

jobs.title: Pricing audit season staff
jobs.role: Partner in a mid-size CA firm
jobs.situation: Demand for audit staff peaks in April–September; freelance rates jump 40%.
steps: The supply of qualified staff is inelastic in the short run (long training).
Plan in advance: train articled assistants, schedule work across the year, use technology.
Expect elasticity to rise in the long run as more people qualify.
jobs.takeaway: Inelastic supply of skilled labour explains seasonal fee spikes; long-run planning raises elasticity.

mcqs.q: Supply refers to:
options: Quantity offered for sale at a price during a period
Quantity produced in a year regardless of price
mcqs.explain: Supply is the quantity of a good that sellers are willing and able to offer for sale at a given price during a given period. "Total stock with the seller" is the trap — stock is everything held, while supply is only the part brought to market at that price. In practice: a cold-storage owner holding 500 tonnes of potatoes may release only 100 tonnes this week, waiting for better prices.

mcqs.q: Stock and supply are equal in the case of:
mcqs.explain: For highly perishable goods such as fresh fish, flowers or milk, sellers cannot hold stock back for a better price, so the entire stock is offered and stock equals supply. "Durable goods" is the trap — durables can be stored, so supply can be far below stock. In practice: vegetable vendors sell off their remaining stock cheaply at the end of the day rather than let it rot.

mcqs.q: Supply is a flow concept because it is:
options: Measured at a point of time
mcqs.explain: Supply is a flow because it is measured per unit of time — tonnes per week, units per month. "Measured at a point of time" is the trap; that describes a stock, such as inventory on 31 March. In practice: a steel company reports production and dispatches per month or quarter, while its balance sheet shows closing stock on a single date.

mcqs.q: A rise in the price of a factor of production, other things constant, will:
mcqs.explain: A higher price of a factor such as wages, raw material or power raises the cost of production, so sellers offer less at every price — supply decreases and the curve shifts left. "Cause expansion of supply" is the trap; expansion is a movement along the curve caused by a rise in the good's own price. In practice: when coal prices spiked, power producers and cement makers cut supply at prevailing prices.

mcqs.q: An improvement in technology will generally:
options: Shift the supply curve to the right
Shift the supply curve to the left
Cause a movement along the supply curve
mcqs.explain: Better technology lowers the cost per unit, so producers can offer more at every price — the supply curve shifts to the right. "A movement along the supply curve" is the trap; movements come only from a change in the good's own price, while technology is a non-price determinant. In practice: drip irrigation and better seeds have raised crop output per acre for Indian farmers at the same prices.

mcqs.q: A farmer grows less wheat when the price of mustard rises. This shows the effect of:
options: Prices of related goods on supply
mcqs.explain: Wheat and mustard compete for the same land; when mustard becomes more profitable, the farmer shifts land to it and supplies less wheat. This is the effect of prices of related goods on supply. "Technology on supply" is the trap — nothing about production methods changed, only relative profitability. In practice: government MSP announcements for rabi crops influence how farmers split their acreage between wheat, mustard and gram.

mcqs.q: If sellers expect the price of a good to rise next month, current supply is likely to:
mcqs.explain: If sellers expect prices to rise next month, they hold back stock to sell later at the higher price, so current supply falls. "Rise" is the trap — that would happen if sellers expected prices to fall and rushed to sell now. In practice: traders hoard onions or pulses when they expect a price rise, which is why the government imposes stock limits during shortages.

mcqs.q: A per-unit subsidy to producers will:
mcqs.explain: A per-unit subsidy reduces the producer's effective cost, so more is offered at every price — supply increases and the curve shifts right. "Cause contraction of supply" is the trap; contraction is a movement down the curve caused by a fall in the good's own price. In practice: the PLI scheme for mobile phones effectively subsidises production, encouraging manufacturers to supply more from India.

mcqs.q: The law of supply states that, other things constant:
options: Quantity supplied varies directly with price
Quantity supplied varies inversely with price
mcqs.explain: The law of supply says that, other things constant, quantity supplied varies directly with price: a higher price brings forth more, because it covers higher marginal costs and promises more profit. "Varies inversely with price" is the trap — that is the law of demand. In practice: when tomato prices jump, farmers in nearby districts rush more produce to the mandis to cash in.

mcqs.q: A supply curve shows:
options: The maximum quantity offered at each price and the minimum price needed for each quantity
mcqs.explain: A supply curve can be read two ways: the maximum quantity sellers will offer at each price, or the minimum price they need to supply each quantity. "The cost of production only" is the trap — costs lie behind the curve, but the curve itself links price and quantity offered. In practice: a contract manufacturer quoting a minimum price for an order of 10,000 units is reading off its own supply curve.

mcqs.q: The market supply curve is obtained by:
options: Horizontal summation of individual supply curves
mcqs.explain: Market supply is found by horizontal summation: at each price, the quantities offered by all individual sellers are added together. "Vertical summation" is the trap — that would add prices at a given quantity, which has no meaning for market supply. In practice: an industry body estimates total sugar supply at a given price by adding the output that each mill is willing to sell.

mcqs.q: An exception to the law of supply is often seen in:
options: Supply of labour at very high wages
mcqs.explain: At very high wages, workers may choose more leisure instead of more work, because their income is already high — so the labour supply curve can bend backwards, an exception to the law of supply. "Supply of wheat" is the trap; ordinary goods like wheat follow the law. In practice: highly paid consultants sometimes cut their working hours once their fees rise beyond a comfortable level.

mcqs.q: Three firms supply 30, 25 and 15 units at ₹40. Market supply at ₹40 is:
mcqs.explain: Market supply at a price is the horizontal sum of the firms' quantities: 30 + 25 + 15 = 70 units at ₹40. 23.33 is the trap — it is the average per firm, not the market total. In practice: commodity analysts estimate total supply by adding production plans of all major producers at the expected price.

mcqs.q: A rise in the price of a good, other things constant, causes:
options: Expansion of supply — upward movement along the curve
mcqs.explain: A rise in the good's own price, other things constant, leads to expansion of supply — an upward movement along the same supply curve. "Increase in supply — rightward shift" is the trap; a shift happens only when a non-price factor changes, such as cost or technology. In practice: when cotton prices rise during the season, ginners and farmers sell more along the existing supply curve.
mcqs.topic: Movements on the Supply Curve – Increase or Decrease in the Quantity Supplied

mcqs.q: A rise in the GST rate on a product will:
options: Shift the supply curve to the left
Shift the supply curve to the right
mcqs.explain: A higher GST rate raises the cost of selling each unit, so at every market price sellers are willing to supply less — the supply curve shifts left. "Cause expansion of supply" is the trap; expansion results from a rise in the good's own price, not from a tax. In practice: when GST rates on certain products are raised, some producers cut output or exit marginal segments.
mcqs.topic: Shifts in Supply Curve – Increase or Decrease in Supply

mcqs.q: An increase in supply means:
options: More is offered at each price
More is offered only because price has risen
Less is offered at each price
mcqs.explain: An increase in supply means sellers offer more at each price — the whole curve shifts to the right because of a non-price factor. "More is offered only because price has risen" is the trap; that is an expansion of supply, a movement along the curve. In practice: a bumper monsoon raises the supply of pulses at every price, which is an increase in supply.
mcqs.topic: Shifts in Supply Curve – Increase or Decrease in Supply

mcqs.q: A vertical supply curve indicates elasticity of supply equal to:
mcqs.explain: A vertical supply curve means quantity supplied stays the same whatever the price, so elasticity of supply = 0 — perfectly inelastic. "Infinity" is the trap; that describes a horizontal supply curve. In practice: the number of seats at a cricket stadium on match day is fixed; however high ticket prices go, supply cannot change.

mcqs.q: A horizontal supply curve shows:
mcqs.explain: A horizontal supply curve means sellers will supply any quantity at the going price but nothing below it — elasticity is infinite, or perfectly elastic. "Perfectly inelastic supply" is the trap; that is a vertical curve. In practice: a small firm buying a standard input such as cement from a large market faces an almost horizontal supply curve — it can buy as much as it wants at the market price.

mcqs.q: A straight-line supply curve passing through the origin has elasticity:
mcqs.explain: For any straight-line supply curve through the origin, q/p equals the slope dq/dp, so elasticity = (dq/dp) × (p/q) = 1 at every point, whatever the slope. "Greater than 1" is the trap — that holds for lines cutting the price axis, not those through the origin. In practice: this geometric shortcut lets an analyst classify supply elasticity from a sketch without any numbers.

mcqs.q: A straight-line supply curve that cuts the quantity axis has elasticity:
mcqs.explain: A straight-line supply curve that cuts the quantity axis has a positive quantity even at zero price, so q/p exceeds the slope and elasticity is less than 1 at every point. "Greater than 1" is the trap — that applies to lines that cut the price axis. In practice: this shape fits goods where some output comes regardless of price, such as farm produce already planted.

mcqs.q: Price rises from ₹500 to ₹550; quantity supplied rises from 2,400 to 3,000. Es is:
mcqs.explain: Es = %ΔQ ÷ %ΔP = ((3,000 − 2,400)/2,400) ÷ ((550 − 500)/500) = 25% ÷ 10% = 2.5, so supply is elastic. 0.4 is the trap — it divides the price change by the quantity change, inverting the formula. In practice: a manufacturer with spare capacity can raise output sharply when prices improve, giving such a high elasticity.

mcqs.q: Supply function q = −200 + 30P. Elasticity of supply at P = ₹20 is:
mcqs.explain: At P = 20, q = −200 + 30 × 20 = 400. Es = (dq/dp) × (P/q) = 30 × 20/400 = 1.5. 30 is the trap — it is only the slope dq/dp, which must be multiplied by P/q; 0.67 inverts the result. In practice: economists estimate supply functions from production data to predict how much extra output a price rise will bring.

mcqs.q: Price rises from ₹45 to ₹60 and supply from 600 to 900 kg. Arc elasticity of supply is:
mcqs.explain: Arc elasticity = (ΔQ ÷ (Q1 + Q2)) × ((P1 + P2) ÷ ΔP) = (300/1,500) × (105/15) = 0.2 × 7 = 1.4. 1.5 is the trap — it uses the original values as base: (300/600) ÷ (15/45). The arc method gives the same answer whichever direction the price moves. In practice: agricultural economists use arc elasticity for large seasonal price swings in crops.

mcqs.q: Elasticity of supply is generally greater in the:
options: It does not depend on time
mcqs.explain: Elasticity of supply is greater in the long run, because firms have time to expand plants, hire and train workers, and new firms can enter. "Market period" is the trap — in that very short period supply is fixed at the stock available, so it is nearly perfectly inelastic. In practice: housing supply responds slowly to rising prices because new projects take years to build.

mcqs.q: Supply is likely to be more elastic when:
mcqs.explain: With spare capacity, firms can raise output quickly without much extra cost, so supply responds strongly to a price rise — it is more elastic. "Inputs are scarce and specialised" is the trap; scarce, specialised inputs make supply less elastic. In practice: during a demand slump, factories running at 60% capacity can scale up fast once orders return.

mcqs.q: Supply of aircraft is less elastic than supply of motorbikes mainly because:
options: Production is complex and takes longer
mcqs.explain: Aircraft production is highly complex, needs specialised inputs and takes years, so output cannot respond quickly to price — supply is less elastic. "Demand for aircraft is elastic" is the trap; elasticity of supply depends on production conditions, not on how demand responds. In practice: Indian airlines that ordered hundreds of aircraft have had to wait years for deliveries, while motorbike makers can step up output within weeks.

mcqs.q: If factors of production are occupationally mobile, elasticity of supply is:
mcqs.explain: When factors such as labour and machines can easily switch between products, output of a good can be raised quickly when its price rises, so elasticity of supply is higher. "Lower" is the trap — immobile, specialised factors are what make supply inelastic. In practice: a garment unit can switch its tailors from shirts to masks within days, as many did in 2020.

mcqs.q: Qd = 500 − 10P and Qs = 50 + 5P. Equilibrium price is:
mcqs.explain: At equilibrium, Qd = Qs: 500 − 10P = 50 + 5P, so 450 = 15P and P = ₹30 (quantity = 200 units on both sides). ₹45 is the trap — it divides 450 by 10 only, ignoring the supply slope. In practice: commodity exchanges discover such equilibrium prices continuously as buy and sell orders are matched.

mcqs.q: At a price above equilibrium, there is:
mcqs.explain: At a price above equilibrium, sellers offer more than buyers want, creating excess supply; unsold stock then pushes sellers to cut prices towards equilibrium. "Excess demand, pushing price up" is the trap — that happens when price is below equilibrium. In practice: when a minimum support price is set above the market price, the government ends up with large procurement stocks that the market would not absorb.

mcqs.q: Producer surplus is:
options: Price received minus the minimum price at which the seller would supply
Price minus consumer's willingness to pay
mcqs.explain: Producer surplus is the price a seller actually receives minus the minimum price at which he would have been willing to supply — shown on a graph as the region lying between the market price line and the supply curve. "Price minus consumer's willingness to pay" is the trap; that relates to consumer surplus, which is the buyer's gain. In practice: a farmer who would sell at ₹1,800 a quintal but receives ₹2,200 enjoys ₹400 of producer surplus.

questions.q: The price of cement rises from ₹1,000 to ₹1,250 a tonne and supply rises from 4,000 to 5,600 tonnes a week. Compute elasticity of supply, classify it, and state two determinants that may explain the result.

model.text: % change in q = 1,600 ÷ 4,000 = 40%; % change in p = 250 ÷ 1,000 = 25%. Es = 40 ÷ 25 = 1.6 — relatively greater elastic.
Possible reasons: spare capacity in cement plants; easy availability of limestone and fuel; many producers competing; the period considered long enough to adjust output.

remarks: Determinants must be of elasticity of supply, not of supply itself.
mistakes: Listing "price of the good" as a determinant of elasticity.

questions.q: The supply function of a firm is q = −50 + 10P. (a) Find point elasticity of supply at P = ₹15. (b) Find arc elasticity between ₹15 and ₹20. (c) Is supply elastic throughout? Explain using the intercept rule.

model.text: (c) Yes. The line q = −50 + 10P cuts the price axis at P = 5 (q = 0), so it starts from the price axis; such a linear supply curve has Es > 1 at every point, approaching 1 as price rises.

elastic throughout|elastic every|elastic at every|elastic all|es 1|greater than 1|more than 1|exceed 1

remarks: Good answers state dq/dp = 10 before substituting.
mistakes: Using the percentage method in (b) instead of the arc formula.
tips: Price-axis intercept → elastic; through origin → unitary; quantity-axis intercept → inelastic.

questions.q: In a market Qd = 1,200 − 20P and Qs = 300 + 10P. (a) Find equilibrium price and quantity. (b) A new technology raises supply by 150 units at every price. Find the new equilibrium. (c) Is (b) an increase in supply or an expansion of supply? Explain.

model.text: (c) It is an increase in supply — the whole supply curve shifts to the right because a non-price determinant (technology) changed. Expansion would mean more supplied only because the good's own price rose. Here the price actually fell while quantity rose.

scheme.pt: New supply function and new equilibrium

kw: increase in supply|increase of supply|increase supply|shift

remarks: Write the new supply function explicitly — it shows the shift.
mistakes: Adding 150 to the equilibrium quantity directly.
tips: Price falls and quantity rises after a rightward supply shift.

checks.label: q3 new equilibrium price after supply rises by 150 at every price

summary: Supply = quantity offered for sale at a price per period; needs willingness and ability; is a flow; ≠ stock.
Determinants: own price, related goods' prices, factor prices, technology, government policy, competition/industry size, expectations, number of sellers.
Law of supply: direct price–quantity relation, ceteris paribus; exception — labour at very high wages.
Own price → expansion/contraction (movement); other factors → increase/decrease (shift).
Types: 0 (vertical), <1, 1, >1, ∞ (horizontal). Line through origin = 1; from price axis > 1; from quantity axis < 1.
remember: Supply is more elastic in the long run, with spare capacity, mobile and available inputs, many producers, storable goods.
Equilibrium: Qd = Qs; above it excess supply, below it excess demand.
traps: A tax or input-cost rise is a leftward shift, not a contraction.
Market supply is a horizontal sum.
Do not confuse stock with supply.

viva.q: What is the difference between an increase in supply and an expansion of supply?
viva.model: An expansion of supply is a rise in quantity supplied caused only by a rise in the good's own price; it is an upward movement along the same supply curve. An increase in supply is caused by a change in some other factor, such as lower costs or better technology, and the whole supply curve shifts to the right so that more is offered at every price.

viva.q: What is elasticity of supply, and when is supply perfectly inelastic?
viva.model: Elasticity of supply is the degree of responsiveness of quantity supplied to a change in price; we measure it as percentage change in quantity supplied over percentage change in price. Supply is perfectly inelastic when quantity supplied does not change at all whatever the price, so elasticity is zero and the supply curve is vertical.

viva.q: Name any four determinants of elasticity of supply.
viva.model: Elasticity of supply depends on the time period, since supply is more elastic in the long run; on spare capacity; on how costs behave as output expands; on the availability and mobility of inputs and how easily factors can be substituted; on the number of producers and ease of entry; on stocks and storability; and on the complexity of production.

viva.q: Why does a straight-line supply curve passing through the origin have unit elasticity?
viva.model: For a straight line through the origin, quantity is proportional to price, so q by p equals dq by dp at every point. Since elasticity equals dq by dp multiplied by p by q, the two ratios cancel and elasticity equals one everywhere.

cases.title: Strawberry season in Mahabaleshwar
cases.case: Strawberry growers in a hill district supply 10,000 kg a week at ₹50 a kg. A heat wave elsewhere raises the price to ₹60. In the first week growers can only pick a little more fruit and supply rises to 10,500 kg. By the end of the season, after extra plots were brought into picking and labour was hired, weekly supply reached 13,000 kg at ₹60. The state government is also considering a subsidy on drip irrigation for growers.

mcqs.q: Elasticity of supply in the first week (percentage method) is:
mcqs.explain: First week: %ΔQ = (10,500 − 10,000)/10,000 = 5%; %ΔP = (60 − 50)/50 = 20%; Es = 5 ÷ 20 = 0.25 — inelastic. 0.05 is the trap: it is only the percentage change in quantity, not divided by the price change; 4 inverts the ratio. In practice: in the very short run, fruit growers can only pick what is already ripe, so supply barely responds to price.

mcqs.q: Elasticity of supply by the end of the season (percentage method) is:
mcqs.explain: End of season: %ΔQ = (13,000 − 10,000)/10,000 = 30%; %ΔP = 20%; Es = 30 ÷ 20 = 1.5 — elastic. 0.3 is the trap — it is the quantity change alone, not divided by the price change; 0.67 inverts the ratio. In practice: given time to hire labour and bring new plots into use, growers respond strongly to a sustained price rise.

mcqs.q: The difference between the first-week and the end-of-season elasticity of supply is best explained by:
options: The time period available to adjust supply
A change in the number of buyers
The law of diminishing marginal utility
mcqs.explain: Supply was inelastic (0.25) in the first week and elastic (1.5) by season-end because growers needed time to hire labour and bring extra plots into picking. Elasticity of supply rises with the time available for adjustment. "A change in the number of buyers" is the trap — that would shift demand, not change how supply responds. In practice: agri-planners expect supply responses to price spikes to build up over a season, not overnight.

mcqs.q: Arc elasticity of supply over the season (₹50/10,000 kg to ₹60/13,000 kg) is:
mcqs.explain: Arc elasticity = (ΔQ ÷ (Q1 + Q2)) × ((P1 + P2) ÷ ΔP) = (3,000/23,000) × (110/10) = 0.1304 × 11 ≈ 1.43. 1.5 is the trap — it is the percentage-method answer using the starting values as base. In practice: analysts prefer the arc method for large price moves, because it gives the same result whether price rises or falls.

mcqs.q: A subsidy on drip irrigation would:
options: Shift the supply curve of strawberries to the right
Cause expansion of supply along the same curve
Shift the demand curve to the right
mcqs.explain: A subsidy on drip irrigation lowers the growers' cost of production — a non-price determinant — so they supply more strawberries at every price: the supply curve shifts right. "Expansion of supply along the same curve" is the trap; expansion needs a rise in the strawberry price itself. In practice: the PM Krishi Sinchayee Yojana subsidises micro-irrigation to raise farm output per drop of water.
